readings.focus: Oz tells the Scarecrow, the Lion and the Tin Woodman that they do not need what they want, then promises to give it to them anyway.
readings.context: Recap: the great Wizard Oz is a humbug, a circus balloonist from Omaha who drifted into this land and let the people believe he was a wizard. He sent Dorothy and her friends to destroy the Wicked Witch of the West because he was afraid of her, and he has just admitted that he cannot keep his promises. Experience is what you learn by doing and living; confidence is trust in yourself.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, from Dorothy calling Oz a bad man to the end of the chapter; opens “"I think you are a very bad man," said Dorothy.”; closes “…to send her back to Kansas, and if he did that she was willing to forgive him everything.”.

questions.prompt: Dorothy calls Oz a very bad man. How does he answer, and do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: He says he is a very good man but a very bad Wizard. Some children agree, since he was kind to his people; others point out that he lied and sent the friends into danger.
evidence: I'm really a very good man; but I'm a very bad Wizard

questions.prompt: Where does Oz say knowledge comes from? Has the Scarecrow been learning on the journey?
facilitatorNotes: From experience, not from brains alone. Children can recall the Scarecrow’s plans, such as covering his friends with straw against the bees.
evidence: Experience is the only thing that brings knowledge

questions.prompt: Oz says true courage is “facing danger when you are afraid.” Why isn’t the Lion satisfied?
facilitatorNotes: He wants the kind of courage that makes him forget he is afraid. Ask which kind is braver: being afraid and going on, or not feeling afraid at all.
evidence: True courage is in facing danger when you are afraid
the sort of courage that makes one forget he is afraid

questions.prompt: Why does Oz agree to give them things he thinks they do not need?
facilitatorNotes: They say they will be unhappy without them, he has played the Wizard so long he may as well go on, and he wants them to keep his secret. Some children call it kindness, others more humbug.
evidence: I have played Wizard for so many years that I may as well continue the part a little longer

readings.title: Oz, chapter XVI: brains, a heart and courage
readings.challenge: Find the jokes hidden in the gifts, and decide whether the gifts are real.
readings.focus: Oz gives the Scarecrow brains of bran and pins, the Tin Woodman a silk heart and the Lion a dish of courage, and then wonders how he can help being a humbug.
readings.context: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion destroyed the Wicked Witch of the West, then found that the great Wizard Oz is a humbug, an ordinary man from Omaha who fools people with tricks. He told the Scarecrow he could already learn, the Lion that he already had courage and the Woodman that a heart makes people unhappy, but they still wanted their gifts, so he promised them. Bran is the husks of grain; “bran-new” plays on brand-new; tinners’ shears are strong scissors for cutting tin.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “The Magic Art of the Great Humbug,” the whole chapter; opens “Next morning the Scarecrow said to his friends:”; closes “…to carry Dorothy back to Kansas, and I'm sure I don't know how it can be done."”.

questions.prompt: What does Oz put in the Scarecrow’s head, and what jokes do the friends make about it?
facilitatorNotes: Bran mixed with pins and needles, which he calls “bran-new brains.” When the Woodman asks about the pins, the Lion says they prove the Scarecrow is sharp, a word that also means clever.
evidence: a lot of bran-new brains
That is proof that he is sharp

questions.prompt: The Tin Woodman asks, “But is it a kind heart?” Why is that his question?
facilitatorNotes: Kindness is what he wants a heart for; he already weeps over beetles. Oz answers “Oh, very!” though the heart is silk and sawdust. Ask whether the answer matters.
evidence: But is it a kind heart?

questions.prompt: Oz says the drink “cannot be called courage until you have swallowed it.” Is he tricking the Lion or telling the truth in a tricky way?
facilitatorNotes: Both can be argued: the dish holds no magic, but Oz says courage is always inside one, as he said the day before. The Lion feels full of courage afterwards.
evidence: courage is always inside one

questions.prompt: Dorothy tells the Scarecrow, “I have always liked you as you were.” What does Oz think the gifts really do?
facilitatorNotes: He smiles because he gave them “exactly what they thought they wanted”: the gifts work because the friends believe in them. Some children say the gifts are fake; others that the friends’ happiness is real.
evidence: I have always liked you as you were
exactly what they thought they wanted

questions.prompt: Why does Oz say it will “take more than imagination” to send Dorothy home?
facilitatorNotes: The friends’ wishes could be met by belief, but Kansas is a real place across a real desert. Her wish is the one a humbug cannot fake.
evidence: it will take more than imagination to carry Dorothy back to Kansas

readings.title: Oz, chapter XVII, part 1: a plan for a balloon
readings.challenge: Follow a problem and its solution step by step.
readings.focus: Oz plans to carry Dorothy over the desert in a balloon filled with hot air, and decides to go with her.
readings.context: Recap: the Wizard Oz turned out to be a humbug, a circus balloonist from Omaha. He gave the Scarecrow brains of bran and pins, the Tin Woodman a silk heart and the Lion a dish of courage, and they are all delighted. But he did not know how to send Dorothy home across the great desert around the Land of Oz. A cyclone is a whirling windstorm, like the one that carried Dorothy’s house to Oz.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, “How the Balloon was Launched,” from the three sad days to Oz asking Dorothy to help him sew; opens “For three days Dorothy heard nothing from Oz. These were sad days for the little girl,…”; closes “…"Now, if you will help me sew the silk together, we will begin to work on our balloon."”.

questions.prompt: How does each friend feel with his new gift? Find one detail for each.
facilitatorNotes: The Scarecrow has wonderful thoughts he will not share because no one else could understand them; the Woodman feels his heart rattling and finds it kinder than his old one; the Lion says he is afraid of nothing on earth. Children may enjoy the Scarecrow’s excuse.
evidence: he would not say what they were because he knew no one could understand them but himself
he felt his heart rattling around in his breast

questions.prompt: Why does Oz think the way across the desert is through the air?
facilitatorNotes: He came in a balloon, and Dorothy came in a cyclone; both arrived through the air.
evidence: You also came through the air, being carried by a cyclone.

questions.prompt: What problem does Oz find with his balloon, how does he solve it, and what danger is left?
facilitatorNotes: There is no gas in the country, so he will use hot air; but if the air cools, the balloon will come down in the desert.
evidence: if the air should get cold the balloon would come down in the desert

questions.prompt: Why does Oz want to go too? Is he running away or going home?
facilitatorNotes: He is tired of being a humbug, shut up in his rooms, and afraid his people will discover him; he would rather be in a circus again. Both readings fit.
evidence: I am tired of being such a humbug
be in a circus again

readings.title: Oz, chapter XVII, part 2: the balloon goes up
readings.challenge: Notice how a small accident changes a whole plan.
readings.focus: The green balloon is filled over a fire, Toto runs off after a kitten, and the ropes break before Dorothy can climb in.
readings.context: Recap: Oz, the humbug Wizard, plans to fly Dorothy across the desert in a balloon filled with hot air, and to go with her, because he is tired of pretending and would like to work in a circus again. Air-tight means letting no air out.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, from sewing the silk to the end of the chapter; opens “So Dorothy took a needle and thread, and as fast as Oz cut the strips of silk into proper…”; closes “…many days they grieved over the loss of the Wonderful Wizard, and would not be comforted.”.

questions.prompt: What greens go into the balloon, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Light green, dark green and emerald green, because Oz fancies matching the colour all around them, even though he knows the city’s green comes from spectacles.
evidence: a strip of light green silk, then a strip of dark green and then a strip of emerald green

questions.prompt: Where does Oz tell his people he is going, and whom does he leave in charge? Why are those surprising?
facilitatorNotes: To visit “a great brother Wizard” in the clouds, which keeps up his pretending to the end, and the Scarecrow is to rule. Children may say the Scarecrow’s new brains earn it, or that Oz picks him because the people think he is wise.
evidence: a great brother Wizard who lived in the clouds
the Scarecrow will rule over you

questions.prompt: Why is Dorothy not in the basket when the ropes break?
facilitatorNotes: Toto ran into the crowd to bark at a kitten, and she would not leave him behind. A dog’s chase changes everything.
evidence: Toto had run into the crowd to bark at a kitten

questions.prompt: The people remember Oz “lovingly.” After all his tricks, were they right to miss him?
facilitatorNotes: He built their beautiful city and was good to them, though he fooled them for years. Some children agree with the people; others think they would feel differently if they knew the truth.
evidence: Oz was always our friend
would not be comforted
